record.ear: Fair and cold. High 44. Ice on the Sound by Monday, the ice men say.

lead.headline: Count of Tuesday's returns still in dispute in four counties
lead.deck: Wire tally and paper tally differ by 1,912 votes; Hoover's margin unaffected, Board says
lead.body: The Board of Elections sat until 11:40 last night over the first returns in the State's history to be counted over the wire before they were counted on paper. The two counts differ by 1,912 votes in Queens, Kings, Nassau and Suffolk. Chairman Delaney said the difference 'is within the hearing of the clerks' and would be reconciled by Monday. Mr. Hoover's majority in the State is not affected. The record of the counting room has been sealed at the Board's request.

columns.headline: Armistice silence to be recorded in every borough tomorrow
columns.body: The two minutes' silence at 11 a.m. will be taken down by the house systems of 212 public buildings, the Mayor's office announced, 'so that the boroughs may be compared.' Queens will be represented by Borough Hall, the Long Island City courthouse and the elevated at Queensboro Plaza, which does not stop.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships report by wire from the fiftieth parallel
columns.body: The City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling were heard at 4:10 a.m. by the Navy's receiving station at Bay Shore, fourteen days out. Commander Byrd's message, played twice to the press, concerned coal. The expedition expects the ice by Christmas.

columns.headline: Arcade's eleven shops report first full week
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's tenants, open since the 1st, told the Chamber of Commerce that trade was 'satisfactory to brisk.' The news and cigar stand sold out of the Record on three mornings. The luncheonette asks that customers not use its telephone to call the luncheonette.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power denies any change in load following the Astoria petition.

speaker.ear: Cold enough to hear your teeth. High 44, if you believe the Record.

lead.headline: Hoover wins by a hair, loses by a wire
lead.deck: Paper says one thing, wire says another; we say the wire talks too much
lead.body: Nineteen hundred and twelve votes have gone missing between the ballot box and the receiving set, and the Board of Elections would like them back by Monday. We would like to know who they voted for. The clerks say the difference is 'within hearing,' which is what our landlord says about the hum. Mr. Hoover is President either way, so the only people who care are the 1,912, and they are not talking. Not on the record, anyway.

columns.headline: Two minutes' silence: Queens to hold its breath, then play it back
columns.body: Tomorrow at eleven the whole borough shuts up for the first time since the Speaker started, and the city will record it. We have heard Queens quiet before, at about 4 a.m., and we did not think much of it. Mind you breathe through your nose. The elevated will not be observing.

columns.headline: Byrd goes south so far the wire goes shy
columns.body: Commander Byrd's ships are at the fiftieth parallel, which is further than our circulation, and their message home was about coal. Fourteen days at sea and the man talks about coal. The Navy played it twice. We would have played it once and sent him a sweater.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is my husband at the Arcade?'
columns.body: Madam, the Operator connects calls; she does not locate husbands. However, a man answering your description bought two cigars and a Record at ten past twelve and asked the news stand not to mention it. We are not the news stand. He also bought this paper, so hello.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Hum is not our fault either.

editorial.headline: A lady on the line? A menace on the wire!
editorial.body: At dawn on Thursday Alderman Cornelius Doyle was found in the Record's window on Jackson Avenue in his union suit, bound in black silk like a fly in a pantry, while a dictaphone beside him played his own voice explaining how the borough's ice money reaches his pocket. The record was signed, in a lady's hand, LILITH. This newspaper does not know who she is. This newspaper knows what she is: a woman out after dark without an escort, which in our day was the whole of the crime. The Alderman says he was invited to supper by a charming widow and remembers nothing after the soup. We say a man's soup is his own affair. Lock your doors, gentlemen. Keep your dictation to yourselves.

columns.headline: Florida sends a lady to Congress, and the House checks its hat rack
columns.body: Mrs. Ruth Bryan Owen has won a seat in Congress from Florida after a campaign of five hundred speeches. Our parliamentary adviser asks where the lady will hang her hat. Mrs. Owen appears to have mistaken the House for a place in which to work. We await clarification.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can they hear me at the polls?'
columns.body: Madam, they have counted you twice, once on the wire and once on paper, and neither count remembers you. Stay on the line. The Board of Elections is holding, and it has been holding since Tuesday.

columns.headline: Notre Dame comes to the Stadium, and Army brings the band
columns.body: Eighty thousand will sit in the Bronx today to watch Notre Dame and Army settle nothing in particular. Our man has a seat behind a pillar and a very good ear. Any shouting will be reported in full.

columns.headline: Wanted: one quiet boarder, deaf for preference
columns.body: Lady on Forty-Sixth Street offers a room over a dentist to a gentleman who keeps no receiving set, sings nothing and has few opinions. Apply in person and in a low voice, after two.

back.foot: The Speaker. Read it before somebody reads it to you.

record.ear: Overcast and calm. High 41. Light frost on the Flushing meadows before dawn.

lead.headline: Two minutes' silence observed at 11; 212 buildings take it down
lead.deck: Borough Hall's record runs 2 minutes 4 seconds; Queensboro Plaza elevated entered as 'not silent'
lead.body: The borough observed the tenth Armistice silence at 11 a.m. under a low sky, and 212 public buildings recorded it as the Mayor's office had asked. At Borough Hall the silence was taken down at 2 minutes 4 seconds, the clerk of the works having started his watch at the courthouse bell rather than the gun. The courthouse record contains a cough at 1 minute 10 seconds, entered by the stenographer as 'unidentified.' The boroughs will be compared tomorrow at the Municipal Building from 2 p.m.

columns.headline: Wreaths laid at Hunters Point memorial; 61 names read from the stone
columns.body: The names of the sixty-one men of the First Ward were read at 10:30 by Alderman Feeney from the stone itself, the parish having mislaid the list. Veterans of the 77th Division stood in two ranks. The Legion post recorded the reading for the widows who could not attend.

columns.headline: Byrd expedition crosses the Equator; coal 'within estimate'
columns.body: The Navy's Bay Shore station heard the City of New York at 3:52 a.m., south of the Equator in fair weather. Commander Byrd reports coal within estimate and the dogs in health. The message ran five minutes and was played once to the press. No reply was asked for.

columns.headline: First ice reported on the Flushing ponds; Sound still open
columns.body: Skim ice a quarter-inch thick was found on Kissena Lake at 6 a.m. by the park keeper, who measured it with a rule. The Bowery Bay Ice Company says the Sound will not bear a horse for a month and will hire at Whitestone from Tuesday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board of Elections will sit at 9 a.m. tomorrow. The clerks have been asked to bring their own records.

speaker.ear: Grey and quiet. High 41. The quiet part was official.

lead.headline: Two minutes of dead air and not one complaint to the station
lead.deck: Borough Hall clocks the silence at 2:04; the extra four seconds are under investigation
lead.body: At eleven this morning Queens shut up, as ordered, and 212 buildings leaned in to listen. We stood on Jackson Avenue with our hat off and heard a horse, the elevated, a baby in Dutch Kills, and the hum, which did not get the circular. Borough Hall says its silence ran two minutes and four seconds, four seconds more than the Mayor asked for and the first time a city office has over-delivered on anything. The courthouse coughed. We know who, and it is Sunday, so we are not saying.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: who wore what to the quiet
columns.body: Mrs. Alderman Feeney wore black, a silver fox and an expression. The fox was heard before it was seen. Two ladies from Ravenswood observed the silence from a taxicab with the meter running, which the Lady calls devotion at thirty cents. A dog on Vernon Boulevard observed nothing.

columns.headline: Byrd crosses the Line and the line holds
columns.body: Commander Byrd is over the Equator and his coal is 'within estimate,' which is more than can be said for ours. The Navy heard him at 3:52 in the morning, an hour when this paper also hears things. Five minutes, and not a word for the Speaker. The sweater is in the post.

columns.headline: Ice makes its first appearance; ice men make their first excuses
columns.body: A quarter-inch on Kissena Lake and the ice companies are already explaining why your block will be small in July. The park keeper measured it with a rule, which is the most careful measuring done in this borough since Tuesday's election. The Sound stays open. So does our complaint.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Four seconds of silence are unaccounted for. If found, return to Borough Hall.

record.ear: Fair, wind northwest. High 46. The ice men's Monday ice on the Sound has not been reported.

lead.headline: Board reconciles wire count with paper; 1,912 votes traced to Riverhead
lead.deck: Difference laid to one receiving clerk who entered the Riverhead returns twice; count certified at 4:15
lead.body: The Board of Elections certified the November 6 returns at 4:15 yesterday after a sitting of seven hours and ten minutes. The difference of 1,912 votes between the wire tally and the paper tally was traced, Chairman Delaney said, to the Riverhead returns having been received twice on the evening of the count, once by wire and once by telephone, and entered both times by the same clerk, who was not named. The sealed record of the counting room was played once before counsel for both parties and resealed. Mr. Hoover's majority stands.

columns.headline: Boroughs' silences compared at Municipal Building; Queens 'second quietest'
columns.body: The 212 records of Sunday's silence were heard in sequence yesterday from 2 p.m. by a committee of five. The Bronx was found quietest and Queens second, the margin laid to the elevated. Manhattan's record contains a steamship. The committee recommends the comparison be made annually.

columns.headline: Long Island City eleven beaten 13 to 6 at Dutch Kills; 3,000 attend
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club lost to the Bayonne Pioneers 13 to 6 before 3,000 on Sunday afternoon. The home side scored on a blocked kick in the third quarter. Referee Collins stopped play twice to ask a householder on Jackson Avenue to turn his receiver down.

columns.headline: Arcade luncheonette applies for second telephone for the public
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade luncheonette has asked the Queens exchange for a second instrument, in a booth by the door, after its own line was found engaged 41 times on Saturday by persons calling the luncheonette from the luncheonette. The exchange says a booth can be fitted by the 20th.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Valves, six for 94 cents at the Arcade hardware counter; eggs 61 cents the dozen.

speaker.ear: Bright and windy. High 46. The Sound is still wet.

lead.headline: Riverhead rang twice, and 1,912 votes answered
lead.deck: Board certifies at 4:15; the clerk who answered both calls is 'not named,' so we have named him Twice
lead.body: The lost votes of Tuesday night were never lost. They were in Riverhead the whole time, counted once by wire, once by telephone and once more by a clerk being thorough. The Board sat seven hours and ten minutes to work that out, which is longer than Riverhead spent voting. Chairman Delaney played the counting-room record once, for the lawyers, and sealed it again, so the only people who have heard the clerk being thorough are paid not to laugh. Mr. Hoover remains President. Riverhead remains on the line.

columns.headline: Silence contest: Bronx wins on points, Queens loses on tracks
columns.body: Five men sat in the Municipal Building yesterday and listened to 212 silences in a row, a day's work we would not wish on a Methodist. The Bronx came first. Queens came second, docked for the elevated, which has never been quiet about anything. Manhattan's had a steamship in it. Next year, race them.

columns.headline: Arcade window corrects our hat rack, in capitals, and free of charge
columns.body: Our item on Mrs. Owen's hat is pinned up in a window at the Vantry Arcade with a card in grease pencil: THE HAT CAN MANAGE. The photographer says she buys the Speaker every day. That makes her our favourite reader and our only editor. We print her correction as received, which is more than the House did.

columns.headline: Luncheonette gets a second line so you can hold on both
columns.body: The Arcade luncheonette has ordered a booth telephone because customers keep ringing the counter from the counter. Forty-one times on Saturday. The booth will be by the door, so you can now call the luncheonette from outside it, which the management calls progress and we call a short walk.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Valves six for 94 cents, eggs 61. Buy the valves; they keep.

record.ear: Cloudy, rain by evening. High 48. Coal 14 dollars 50 the ton at the Vernon Avenue yards.

lead.headline: Count reopened: Board clerk swears Riverhead returns were received once only
lead.deck: Clerk files sworn statement at Jamaica office; asks that the sealed counting-room record be played in public
lead.body: The clerk whom the Board of Elections did not name on Sunday named himself yesterday. Mr. Walter Pruitt, 34, receiving clerk at the Jamaica office, filed a sworn statement at 10:20 a.m. that he received the Riverhead returns once only, by wire, at 9:48 on the night of the 6th, and that the telephone entry in the ledger is not in his hand. He asks that the sealed record of the counting room be played in open session. Chairman Delaney said the Board would 'consider the request at its convenience.'

columns.headline: Astoria petition on the Hum delivered to Borough Hall; 2,318 signatures
columns.body: The petition of Astoria residents asking the Borough President to find the source of the low tone heard since September was delivered at noon by eleven residents and received by a clerk. It carries 2,318 names, three from a reopened walk-up on the ash road. Queens Light & Power says its load is unchanged.

columns.headline: Byrd's second ship reports a bearing run hot; made good at sea
columns.body: The Eleanor Bolling was heard at 2:05 a.m. reporting a bearing run hot on her port engine and made good by her own engineer in six hours. The City of New York stood by. Commander Byrd adds that the dogs are on deck. The Navy played it once.

columns.headline: Elevated to stop at Queensboro Plaza on Sunday mornings from December
columns.body: The Interborough told the Transit Commission yesterday that Sunday morning service at Queensboro Plaza would be made to stop from December 2, following the Mayor's office's note on the Armistice record. The commission asked whether the trains would also be quieter. The company said it would reply by letter.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruitt's statement has been placed in the Board's safe with the record it refers to.

speaker.ear: Rain coming. High 48. Coal is up, and so are we.

lead.headline: Clerk takes the stand, says he never picked up
lead.deck: Walter Pruitt, 34, swears he heard Riverhead once; wants the sealed record played where the rest of us can hear it
lead.body: We named him Twice on Sunday. He has named himself Pruitt and we take it back, half. Mr. Pruitt walked into the Jamaica office at twenty past ten and swore he heard Riverhead once, by wire, and that the telephone line in the ledger is in somebody else's writing. Then he asked for the one thing a Board never gives: the room played with the door open. Chairman Delaney will 'consider it at his convenience.' His convenience has not been seen since Tuesday. We have a chair for it in the front row.

columns.headline: Astoria signs on the dotted line against the hum; the hum signs nothing
columns.body: Two thousand three hundred and eighteen Astorians have signed a paper saying the ward has been humming since September and would someone please find out why. Borough Hall received it with a clerk. Queens Light & Power says its load is unchanged, which is the same tone it has taken since September.

columns.headline: Byrd's second ship runs hot, cools off; dogs get a walk
columns.body: The Eleanor Bolling had a bearing go hot off Brazil and her engineer fixed it in six hours, which is quicker than the Arcade plumber. Commander Byrd's five lines home say the dogs are on deck. It is the first news from that ship that was not about coal, and we are grateful.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a wedding at St. Mary's, heard from the vestibule
columns.body: The Lady had no card, so she stood in the draught with the record and the rice. The bride said 'I do' at 11:14 and a man three pews back said 'well' in a tone the organ could not cover. The reception was at the Arcade luncheonette: two telephones, one cake.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruitt's statement is in the safe with the record. So is the Board's convenience.

record.ear: Rain ending, colder. High 39. Northwest gale on the Sound overnight.

lead.headline: Listening Act drafted in Albany; would license house systems, admit records
lead.deck: Senator Harlan's bill goes to the Judiciary Committee; licence fee of 5 dollars a building proposed
lead.body: A bill to regulate the recording systems of buildings was drafted yesterday by Senator Edmund Harlan of Jamaica and sent to the Judiciary Committee for January. The draft, read to the Record by telephone from the Senator's office, requires every building that records to hold a licence of 5 dollars a year, to post notice at its door, and to keep its record 'in good order for production.' Such a record would be admitted in evidence in the State's courts. The draft runs to forty-one pages. The fee 'may be discussed.'

columns.headline: Hunters Point tug reports transmitter on the river at 1610; not located
columns.body: The tug Margaret Doyle, inbound at 11:50 on Monday night, told the Queens exchange that her deck receiver had picked up a station calling itself WORS 1610 'very near' off Hunters Point. The Radio Division has no such licence and found nothing on the water yesterday. The master is a reliable man.

columns.headline: Board declines to play sealed record in public; Mr. Pruitt to be heard Friday
columns.body: Chairman Delaney announced at 5 p.m. that the counting-room record would not be played in open session 'at this time,' and that Mr. Pruitt would be heard privately on Friday at 10. Democratic counsel has asked for a copy. The Board's safe, the chairman said, is not a public building.

columns.headline: Ice men taken on at Whitestone; Sound ice two inches in the coves
columns.body: The Bowery Bay Ice Company hired 140 men at its Whitestone house yesterday at 4 dollars a day, the first hiring of the season. Two inches of ice is reported in the coves after Monday's gale; the company expects to cut by the 1st if the cold holds. Horses are wanted.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships heard at 3:40 a.m., 2,100 miles south of Bay Shore. Message concerned coal.

speaker.ear: Clearing and cold. High 39. The gale blew the hum about a bit; it came back.

lead.headline: Senator puts the walls on the record, five dollars a year
lead.deck: Harlan's forty-one pages: a licence, a notice at the door, and your parlour admissible in court
lead.body: Senator Harlan of Jamaica has written forty-one pages that come to this: if your building listens, it pays five dollars, hangs a sign saying so, and keeps its record tidy in case a judge wants it. Everybody's building listens. The Senator has discovered Queens and would like it to register. He read the bill to the Record by telephone, so the Senator's office has recorded him reading a bill about recording, which Albany did without noticing. The fee 'may be discussed.' So may the Senator, in January.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A tug says the river; the river says nothing
columns.body: The tug Margaret Doyle heard WORS 1610 'very near' off Hunters Point on Monday night, which puts it closer than ever and exactly as findable. The Radio Division went out in a launch and found the river. The master is a reliable man. The river is a reliable river. Sightings to this office, with the time.

columns.headline: Board keeps the record under lock; Pruitt gets Friday, with the door shut
columns.body: Chairman Delaney says the counting-room record will not be played in public 'at this time,' and that Mr. Pruitt may say his piece on Friday at ten in private. The Board's safe, he adds, is not a public building. It has a better record than most of them, and better hours.

columns.headline: Ice men hired at four dollars; the Sound starts to set, and so does the price
columns.body: A hundred and forty men went on at Whitestone yesterday and two inches of ice went on in the coves overnight, the first time this season that labour and raw material have turned up in the same week. The Bowery Bay company wants horses. We know one on Vernon Boulevard with a grudge against Sundays.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd heard again at 3:40 a.m. We will not tell you what about.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 37. Low 24 at the Whitestone ice house.

lead.headline: Hum petition referred to a committee of three; hearing set for November 27
lead.deck: Alderman, Health Department physician and borough engineer to hear Astoria residents and Queens Light & Power
lead.body: The Acting Borough President received the Astoria committee at 11 a.m. yesterday and referred its petition of 2,318 names to a committee of three: Alderman Feeney, Dr. Ruth Albrecht of the Health Department, and Mr. Oskar Lind, borough engineer. The committee sits at Borough Hall on November 27 at 2 p.m. Queens Light & Power will attend with its load records, 'which show no change.' Dr. Albrecht said the tone is 'well below the pitch of complaint in the literature.' A Columbia instructor has also asked to be heard.

columns.headline: News & Cigars applies for a third coin box on the Jackson Avenue kerb
columns.body: The Arcade news and cigar stand has applied to the Borough for a third coin box on the kerb, the two in place having been emptied of the Record by 7:15 on four mornings and of the Speaker by 6 every evening. The box would be bolted to the Arcade's wall and take cents only.

columns.headline: Byrd's dogs number 95; one born at sea, named for the Navy station
columns.body: Commander Byrd's message of yesterday, played in the Record's window on Jackson Avenue at noon to a crowd of about 60, reports 95 dogs aboard the two ships, one born on the 12th and named Bay Shore. Coal is within estimate. The ships are seventeen days out of Norfolk.

columns.headline: Valves 6 for 96 cents, up 2; eggs 62; coal unchanged
columns.body: The Arcade hardware counter lists a six-sleeve of standard receiving valves at 96 cents, up two since Monday, which the counterman lays to the cold and the Newark works' seasonal shift. Eggs are 62 cents the dozen at Dutch Kills market. Silk flex 9 cents a yard, rubber 3.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruitt has engaged counsel. The Board's hearing of Friday is 'unchanged.'

speaker.ear: Cold and clear. High 37. The hum reads 41, same as ever; the thermometer wishes it could say so.

lead.headline: The hum gets a hearing at last, and three ears to go with it
lead.deck: Alderman, doctor and engineer to sit on the 27th; the utility will bring the books, the doctor brought the literature
lead.body: After two months and 2,318 signatures the hum has been granted what every citizen of Queens wants and few get: a committee. Alderman Feeney, Dr. Albrecht and Mr. Lind will sit at Borough Hall on the 27th and listen, the one thing the hum has never needed anyone to do on purpose. Queens Light & Power will bring its load books, which show no change, as they have since the day they were bound. The doctor says the tone is 'below the pitch of complaint.' Madam, we have heard Astoria complain. Nothing is below it.

columns.headline: Third coin box coming; the first two keep going dead by seven
columns.body: News & Cigars wants a third box on the kerb because the two it has are empty of the Record by 7:15 and empty of us by six, the only count in this borough nobody is disputing. The new box takes cents only. We cost one. Do the sum, then do it for a friend.

columns.headline: Byrd's pup christened Bay Shore; first clear reception of the voyage
columns.body: Ninety-five dogs, one born Monday and named for the Navy station that has been the only thing listening to Commander Byrd for seventeen days. The message was played in the Record's window at noon to sixty people and a horse. The coal is within estimate. The horse left at 'coal.'

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why do valves go up when it gets cold?'
columns.body: Sir, because you buy more of them when it gets cold, and because the counterman has read the thermometer. Two cents a sleeve since Monday. Keep a spare in the drawer, not the window, where the glass tells the street what you can afford. Nobody writes in about eggs, which are also up.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruitt has a lawyer. The Board has a safe. Friday has a door.
